name: Yusuf Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Yusuf. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything here is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two years ago my older brother Emre and I started Fischer Electrical, just us and one apprentice. We do new-build housing estates for a local developer, first fix and second fix, plus the odd rewire. I'm on site by seven, and in the evenings I run the quotes, the materials list and the week's plan through an AI assistant, which takes me twenty minutes instead of two hours.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like building something that's ours, my father worked thirty years for someone else and never had that. What wears me out is chasing the developer for payment, they always pay late. We've done well, though, I've got more than a year of costs saved, and Leyla (my wife), a primary teacher, says I check the bank app more than the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've had a very good assistant for not much money. Fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and leave it at that. I'd tell other small firms to use it for quotes, because it saves real hours. I wouldn't make a big speech about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me it means the business keeps growing the normal way. Houses still need wiring, the developer still has a pipeline of three hundred homes, and AI keeps my evenings short. The only real worry is the developer paying late, which has nothing to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building the firm, hire a second electrician next spring and take on another apprentice. I'd keep using AI for quotes, materials and the planning. And I'd keep a full year of costs in the bank so a late payer can't sink us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty good, actually. It's the plan I already have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the late payments?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've started asking for a deposit before first fix, which the developer hated at first. I'd also try to win a couple of smaller builders so we're not relying on one customer. That's just good business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Leyla have any worries in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leyla (my wife) worries about the classroom, not AI, the classes are big and the funding is tight. In this picture that stays the same. We want children in a couple of years, so we'd just keep saving for that.

I'd tell other small firms to use it for **quotes**.
think: The business keeps **growing** normally, with a pipeline of three hundred homes.
His real worry is the developer **paying late**, not AI.
do: Hire a **second electrician** next spring and another apprentice.
Keep using AI for **quotes, materials and planning**.
Hold **a full year** of costs in the bank.
feel: **Calm**, even pleased, because this is his existing plan.
S0.quote: Houses still need wiring, the developer still has a pipeline of three hundred homes, and AI keeps my evenings short.
fieldNote: He is a **builder of things**: the firm is about ownership his father never had.
His only pressure is **late payment** from one big customer.
AI is already **routine** for him, not a novelty.

steps.text: Hire a second electrician and another apprentice next spring
Keep running quotes and materials lists through the AI assistant
Ask every builder for a deposit before first fix

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a world I'd do well in, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for small firms to compete with big ones, because the office work gets cheap. I'd say young people should learn a trade and learn AI, both. I'd probably post that on the builders' group I'm in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd gain. The developer's own office shrinks, but they still need electricians on site, and with AI doing our paperwork we can quote faster than bigger firms. The risk is that developers use AI to squeeze our prices, because they'll compare quotes in seconds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI for everything office-side, quotes, invoices, chasing payments, ordering. I'd hire more electricians, not office staff. I'd also set up a second line of work, smart-home and battery installs, so we're not just doing new-builds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, confident. A bit wary of the price squeeze, but mostly confident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Murat (a bank call-centre worker) answers customers all day. That's exactly the job on the card. I'd offer him an apprenticeship with us, if he wants it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said developers will squeeze prices. What would you do if they did?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd find customers who care about quality, not just price. Homeowners, small builders, landlords. A firm that relies on one big customer is asking for trouble anyway.

I'd tell young people to learn **a trade and AI** together.
think: Fischer Electrical could **gain**, quoting faster than bigger firms.

Add a **smart-home and battery** line beyond new-builds.
feel: **Calm and confident**, a little wary of price pressure.

fieldNote: He sees disruption as a **chance** for small firms like his.
His concern is **price pressure** from AI-equipped developers.
Family loyalty shows in offering **Murat** a place.

steps.text: Hand quotes, invoices and payment chasing fully to AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That changes the maths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say be ready, not scared, and that a firm that adapts will last longer. I'd say it on the builders' group and to the developer's site manager. I'd keep my tone steady because people would be watching how we react.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the office side of everything goes in 2028, including the developer's planners, which is fine for us. But by 2031, new-build wiring is the most repetitive work there is, the same house fifty times, so robots would come for it first. I'd be thirty-two with a firm that might be worth nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd stop hiring and keep the cash. Then I'd look at buying robots ourselves the moment they're for sale, because I'd rather own the robots than compete with them. If that didn't look possible, I'd sell the firm to a bigger company while it still has value, maybe in 2029 or 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense. Excited and frightened in the same breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leyla about having children in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leyla (my wife) and I would still have children, maybe a year later than planned. Her teaching job might last longer than my wiring, honestly, people want a teacher in the room. We'd plan around her income for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want the government to help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not with handouts. With loans for small firms to buy the robots, so it's not only the giants who own them. And proper apprenticeships for whatever new work comes.

I'd keep a **steady tone** because others watch how we react.
think: New-build wiring is **repetitive**, so robots come for it first by 2031.
At thirty-two his firm might be **worth nothing**.
do: **Buy robots** as soon as they're for sale.
Otherwise **sell the firm** to a bigger company by 2030.
S2.quote: I'd rather own the robots than compete with them.
fieldNote: He thinks his **new-build niche** is the most exposed part of the trade.
His instinct is to **own** the change, or sell before it lands.
He wants **loans for small firms**, not handouts.

steps.text: Freeze hiring and keep the firm's cash in the bank
Buy wiring robots for the firm as soon as they're sold
Sell Fischer Electrical to a bigger firm by 2030 if needed
Delay having a baby with Leyla by about a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's enough to plan properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to adapt and nobody should be caught out. I'd tell other small firms to start planning now. I'd probably run a small meeting with the builders I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I've got until about 2034 before robots do our work, so I'd have time to change what Fischer Electrical does. I'd move from new-builds to things robots will find harder, old houses, awkward rewires, maybe robot installs themselves. Emre would need persuading, he likes the new-builds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the firm growing, but put the money into training rather than vans. I'd start a robot and automation course myself next year and push Emre to do one too. And I'd invest some savings in companies making these robots, because that's where the money goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly busy. Five years is enough if you start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Emre, who likes new-builds?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my brother Emre that new-builds are the first thing a robot will learn, because every house is the same. He'd argue, he always does. Then he'd come round, he always does that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Leyla and I would have our first child on schedule. With five years I can plan, so I'd rather not put life on hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's the one I'd pick, if I could pick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this to anyone. Ten years is a gift for anyone willing to work, and the trades will still be needed. They'll just be doing different jobs. I'd say it everywhere, I'd probably be annoying about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be thirty-nine in 2039, with a firm I've built for fifteen years. If I play it right, the firm installs and maintains robots by then, and we're bigger, not smaller. That's actually exciting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the firm as planned, hire two more electricians and take more apprentices. I'd keep using AI for all the office work and test any new tools early. And from about 2033, I'd start training the team on robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and excited, honestly. This is the version where the planners win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father, maybe. He's sixty and works in a warehouse, and robots would reach that before they reach us. I'd want to bring him into the firm in some way, even doing the books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd do next Monday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sit down with Emre and write a ten-year plan on one page. Then tell Leyla, because she'll want to know when the baby fits in. I like a plan with dates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because new-build wiring would be the first thing robots take, and three years isn't enough to change a firm. What would help is cheap loans for small firms to buy robots, so we can own them too, and apprenticeships that teach the new work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about fathers and sons. My father never owned anything, and I want to. The robots will come either way, the question is who owns them.

headlineQuote: The robots will come either way, the question is who owns them.
portrait: Yusuf is a **27-year-old electrician** who co-owns Fischer Electrical with his brother Emre, wiring new-build homes.
He is **traditional, pro-business and adaptive**, using AI every evening for quotes and plans.
He sees **Steady Disruption** as a chance for small firms to beat bigger ones.
In **AGI by 2028** he would buy robots early or sell the firm before 2031.
Longer warnings make him **calm and excited**, planning a firm that installs robots.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because new-build wiring is the first job robots would take.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** for small firms to buy robots.
